attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s velocity y and acceleration y so it jumps when the A button is pressed, then falls back to the ground?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when you change a sprite’s velocity y value?

❓ What happens when you change a sprite’s acceleration y value?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the physics concepts they learned during Level 1. Changing a sprite’s velocity y impacts how quickly (and in what direction) a sprite will move from point A to point B. Changing a sprite’s acceleration y impacts how much the sprite’s speed will change (and in what direction) over a certain period of time.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to jump onto the platform and fall back down to the tilemap ground. 


Drag a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on start] container, select the Player sprite’s name, select [ay (acceleration y)] from the drop down, and type 500 as the parameter. This will create “gravity” that pulls the sprite back to the ground.


Drag out an [on button pressed] container into the editor. Then, add a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on button pressed] container. Click the dropdown and select [vy (velocity y)], then set the parameter to -250. Add an [if then] conditional to the [on button pressed] container so the Player sprite can only jump if it’s standing on the ground. Replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> value block. Click the drop down and select [bottom]. 


Click ▶ then press the A button to see that the Player sprite is only able to jump when the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a (location) bubble into the <tile at location is tile> block and select the reward tile ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you think the <tile at location is tile> block might be useful in a project? 

❓ How do you think it will be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The tilemap collision blocks can be helpful for checking to see if a specific tile was hit by the Player sprite, and cause an action to happen as a result. In this project, hitting the reward tile will replace the tile with a wall tile and change the score by 1.
steps.instructions:
Change the score when the Player sprite overlaps a reward tile.


Add an [if then] conditional into the [on sprite hits wall] container and replace the <true> value with a <tile at location is tile> block. Then, drag a (location) bubble into the coordinate parameter, and select the reward tile from the drop down.


Drag a [set tile at location] block inside the conditional. Select the brick platform tile, then drag the (location) bubble into the coordinate parameter. Add a [change score by] block underneath.


Click ▶ to see the reward tile turn into a brick platform tile and the score change by 1 when the Player sprite overlaps it.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an <and> Boolean to check if the tile to the top of the Player sprite is the reward tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What needs to be true in order for the reward tile to turn into a brick platform tile?

❓ Why do you think it’s necessary to include both <tile at location is tile> and <tile at to [top] of sprite is tile> blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡In this example, it is necessary to use both <tile at location is tile> and <tile at to [top] of sprite is tile> blocks in the <and>. By only using one, the project often triggers 2 tiles to turn into a brick platform, if the Player sprite is not perfectly aligned underneath.
steps.instructions:
Code the reward tile to turn into a brick platform tile only when the Player sprite hits it from below! 


Open Logic and replace the <tile at location is tile> block with an <and> Boolean. Drag the <tile at location is tile> block back into the left parameter.


Add a <tile to [left] of sprite is tile> block into the right parameter of the <and> Boolean. Select [top] from the drop down, the Player sprite’s name, and the reward tile. This will check if the tile at the top of the Player sprite is the reward tile.


Click ▶ to see that the reward tile only turns into a brick platform tile when the Player sprite jumps up and hits it from below.

steps.hints: ❓Did you program the Food sprite to appear, float up, and destroy on wall when it hits the top of the screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens now when the top of the Player sprite hits a reward tile?

❓ Have you seen this type of interaction in any other games that you know?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja may make a connection to games like Super Mario Bros., where the top of a Player sprite hits a wall tile to make something pop up. Prompt the ninja to consider how else this interaction might be used in a project.
steps.instructions:
Code a Food sprite to appear when the reward tiles are hit by the Player sprite! 


Create a Food sprite inside the conditional by adding a [set sprite to] block set to a coin image and the Food sprite kind. Set the Food sprite’s position with a [place sprite on top of] block set to the (location) bubble. 


Set the Food sprite to move by dragging a [change sprite [x] by] block into the conditional, selecting [vy (velocity y)], and typing -50 in the parameter. Destroy the Food sprite when it floats all the way to the top of the screen by using a [set sprite [auto destroy]] block set to [destroy on wall] with the toggle <ON>. 


Click ▶ to see the Food sprite appear, float up, and increase the score only when the Player sprite hits a reward tile from below.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an <and> Boolean to check if the Player sprite is overlapping with the Enemy sprite, and if the score is a certain number?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What needs to happen in order for the game to end in a win?

❓ How is the <(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)> block similar and different from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container?

❓ What does the <and> Boolean allow you to do in a game? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to compare the <(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)> block with the overlap container they are already familiar with. Have the ninja notice that the container uses a sprite kind to identify an overlap event, whereas the <(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)> block simply checks if a specific sprite is overlapping with another single sprite.

💡Prompt the ninja to consider the benefit of using two conditions to cause an action to occur and other ways they might incorporate the <and> Boolean into a project.
steps.instructions:
End the game by bringing the Enemy sprite 7 coins!


Drag an [if then] conditional into the empty [forever] loop. Replace the <true> value with an <and> Boolean. Open Sprites and drag a <(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)> block into the left parameter of the <and> Boolean. Replace (mySprite) and (otherSprite) with the Player and Enemy sprite names.


Drag a <0=0> comparison block into the right parameter. Click the drop down to select (≥). Drag a (score) variable into the left parameter of the <0≥0> comparison block, then type 7 in the right parameter. Add a [game over] block inside the conditional, set the toggle to <WIN>, and use a [use effect] block to add a win effect.


Click ▶ and collect all 7 coins, then find the Enemy Sprite to win the game.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box and updating any sound or visual effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Magic Coin Scavenger Hunt
subgroups.introduction: Create a platformer project with a 2D tilemap that uses logic operators to uncover hidden sprites!

validationItems.text: Player sprite jumps up when the A button is pressed and the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall.
Change the score and tile when the Player sprite jumps up to hit a reward tile.
A Food sprite appears from the reward tile, moves to the top of the screen, then is destroyed by the wall.
End the game when the Player sprite collects 7 coins AND overlaps the Enemy sprite.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Sound and visual effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about Booleans and logic operators. Booleans can be useful to check if specific and/or multiple conditions have been met in a project. They can also be useful in 2D platformer projects to keep track of certain game conditions and to make something happen on certain tilemap events. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: It All Keeps Adding Up
badges.description: Use logic and math to make different things happen in a project.

badges.title: All or Nothing
badges.description: Check if two conditions are both true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Fork in the Road
badges.description: Check if one of two conditions is true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Nuh-Uh!
badges.description: Check for the negative, or opposite, of a variable’s current value.

badges.title: Yes/No Question
badges.description: Set a condition using the Boolean values true or false.

badges.title: Knowing Your Surroundings
badges.description: Check for the tile next to a sprite before making something happen in a project.

badges.title: Splat!
badges.description: Set a sprite to be destroyed whenever it touches a tilemap wall.

badges.title: Math Magician
badges.description: Perform a mathematical operation in a project’s code.
